svg.aria-label: Diagram: health checks for instances in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. All instances start with a Healthy status and are assumed healthy unless Auto Scaling receives notification that they are unhealthy, and when it determines that an InService instance is unhealthy it replaces it with a new instance to maintain desired capacity. Five sources can report unhealthy: Amazon EC2 status checks and scheduled events, which are the default health check type and are always enabled with no special configuration and no way to remove them; Elastic Load Balancing health checks, which by default Auto Scaling ignores and which must be turned on; VPC Lattice health checks, likewise ignored by default; Amazon EBS health checks, which must be turned on; and custom health checks you define. Application status checks are different again: they extend the EC2 status check signal to your application over HTTP or HTTPS, and no additional Auto Scaling group configuration is required, so they take effect without the group opting in. The response to a failing EC2 status check is deliberately patient. Auto Scaling lets the status checks fail occasionally without taking any action, waits a few minutes for AWS to fix the issue, does not immediately mark an instance Unhealthy when its status becomes impaired, and does not mark the instance Unhealthy if a status check returns insufficient-data. That delay is the window in which EC2 automatic instance recovery migrates the instance to another host, which is why recovery and replacement do not fight each other. The exception is decisive: if Auto Scaling detects that an instance is no longer in the running state, this is treated as an immediate failure and it immediately marks the instance Unhealthy and replaces it, including during the health check grace period, so stopping an instance in an Auto Scaling group gets it replaced. Scheduled events also cause replacement, and where Auto Scaling has high confidence the instance is impaired, for example degraded GPUs, replacement occurs immediately, otherwise it waits for the scheduled event to begin. The grace period is the trap: the health check grace period specifies the minimum amount of time in seconds to keep a new instance in service before terminating it if it is found to be unhealthy, and in the console the default is 300 seconds, while its default value is 0 seconds when you create an Auto Scaling group using the AWS CLI or an SDK, where a value of 0 turns off the health check grace period. Setting the value too high reduces the effectiveness of the health checks. Replacement is throttled: Auto Scaling only replaces up to 10 percent of the group's desired capacity at a time, waits for in-progress scaling activity when the group is under desired capacity by 10 percent or more, and if 10 percent of the group is less than one it replaces unhealthy instances one at a time, which might result in some downtime for the group. Finally, replacement discards what recovery preserves: when an instance is terminated, any associated Elastic IP addresses are disassociated and are not automatically associated with the new instance, and attached EBS volumes are detached or deleted. Instances in Standby state are not health checked until returned to service, and the only way to stop replacement entirely is to suspend the ReplaceUnhealthy and HealthCheck processes.
svg.title: The console gives you 300 seconds of grace; the API gives you none
svg.text: Two defaults for one setting, and your IaC got the zero.
“In the console, by default, the health check grace period is 300 seconds … Its default value is 0 seconds
when you create an Auto Scaling group using the AWS CLI or an SDK. A value of 0 turns off the…”
Five sources, and only one is on without asking
EC2 status checks + scheduled events DEFAULT · “always enabled” · cannot be removed
Elastic Load Balancing ignored by default · must be turned on
VPC Lattice ignored by default · must be turned on
Amazon EBS must be turned on
Custom (set-instance-health) yours to call
Why replacement does not fight recovery
“Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling lets the status checks fail occasionally, without taking any action. When a
status check fails, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling waits a few minutes for AWS to fix the issue.”
That pause is the window automatic recovery uses to migrate the instance. It also ignores
insufficient-data, so a missing datapoint is not a replacement.
The one condition with no patience and no grace
“if Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling detects that an instance is no longer in the running state, this situation is
treated as an immediate failure.”
True during the grace period too — so stopping an instance to debug it replaces it instead.
REPLACEMENT IS THROTTLED
“only replaces up to 10 percent of the group’s
desired capacity at a time”
Under 10 instances → one at a time, and
“might result in some downtime for the group”.
WHAT REPLACEMENT LOSES
“any associated Elastic IP addresses are
disassociated and are not automatically
associated with the new instance”
Recovery keeps the address. Replacement does not.
Degraded GPUs are named in the docs: where confidence is high the instance is impaired, “replacement occurs immediately”.
Application status checks need no group configuration at all, so they can start causing replacements without anyone
editing the Auto Scaling group — unlike the load balancer checks, which are ignored until switched on.
EC2 checks cannot be removed; to stop replacement you suspend the ReplaceUnhealthy and HealthCheck processes.
